analysis.title: GS Kaplan - GS Global Equities Call 16 Nov 2026
key_insights: US equities are lower to start the week (SPX futures -35bps, NDX -90bps, RTY -35bps, UST 10-year unchanged at 5.135%, WTI -60bps at $88). AI-related names lead the weakness: NVDA -2.6% pre-market, DRAM -5%, SMH -3%, Neoclouds -6%, Tokyo Electron -7%, Hynix -7.8% locally, TSMC -5.7%.

The desk sees no single trigger for the AI selloff. The market is digesting possible implications of NVDA without Jensen Huang (capex cycle duration, NVDA's financial support for Neoclouds, possible changes to AI chip export rules) ahead of NVDA's EPS print on Tuesday. Bessent urged NVDA over the weekend to pursue a 'dramatic' shakeup and look externally for its next CEO, and the FT reported Huang is discussing a possible return.

The week is heavy on AI catalysts and consumer earnings: NVDA and MSFT Ignite on Tuesday, BABA on Thursday, TSN and ARMK Monday, HD Tuesday, TJX, TGT and LOW Wednesday, WMT, ROST and GAP Thursday, BJ Friday. Macro is slower, with US Retail Sales Tuesday and FOMC minutes Wednesday. The Q3 13F deadline is tonight.
GS Week Ahead puts the S&P implied move through Friday 11/20 at 1.72%. The APEC summit in Shenzhen runs Wednesday to Thursday, with Trump holding bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday.

Coppersmith says AI sentiment is about as negative as it has been in quite some time, and it now shows in positioning and valuations. He still thinks equities can grind higher after the positioning reset but prefers to be more selective. He would use weakness in parts of AI to add rather than chase rallies, expects rotation beyond infrastructure into next year, and would stay disciplined on hedges because AI spending growth is peaking and financing is getting more expensive.
CTAs have been aggressively selling Tech and NDX CTA positioning is back near max short levels. Coppersmith says it probably does not take much positive news to spark a squeeze higher.

Semis have underperformed the S&P by more than 30 percentage points since June, the sharpest relative drawdown since 2002 but short of the 1990s extremes. GS Research argues much of this has gone too far, with some stocks discounting close to zero earnings growth in 2028.

The GS AI Semis basket (GSCBSMHX) trades at 11x 2028 earnings against nearly 16x for the S&P, while consensus expects 31% earnings growth in 2028. At the S&P multiple, current prices would imply earnings declining about 6%. So either the selloff has gone too far or investors are already pricing in estimate cuts.

GS Global Macro Outlook 2027: global growth was 2.7% in 2026 and GS expects 2.8% in 2027, as lower energy prices and strong AI capex outweigh tighter financial conditions and more neutral fiscal policy. Risks are tilted to the downside: renewed Iran escalation and another energy spike, large fiscal deficits lifting long-term yields (especially France), and AI capex disappointing because of capacity constraints, regulation, credit stress or weaker demand. There are early signs AI is weighing on the job market.

GS expects inflation to slow in 2027 as tariff pass-through ends, the energy impulse fades and AI-related pressures ease, though risks on energy and AI pass-through are to the upside. GS expects two more Fed hikes and one ECB hike, then a return to cuts in late 2027. Longer-term rates are expected to come down modestly. With the highest real yields in years, bonds are starting to regain hedging value, and longer-dated index options can offer portfolio protection because equity index volatility is more likely to rise than fall.

GS Global Markets Outlook 2027 lists 10 themes: a maturing market cycle, an AI investment impulse that peaks, equity leadership passing from AI infrastructure to other areas, energy risk and risk premium, bonds regaining macro and hedging value, a softer and more cyclical Dollar (especially against JPY and CNY), European pressure until the French election (EUR downside attractive), the stress of financing the boom with further US credit spread widening likely, EM resilience and diversification, and growth risks that call for tail hedges.

GS Global Equities Strategy 2027: earnings growth is set to slow (US from 36% to 11%, Europe from about 18% to 7%, Japan from 24% to 9%, Asia from close to 80% to under 30%) as hyperscaler capex growth slows and energy prices moderate. Cost of capital is higher. Focus areas are Growth over Value (value within technology, especially hyperscalers, plus semis and some consumer cyclicals), selective defensives (Europe Utilities and Telecoms, US Healthcare and consistent buyback names, Asian power) and selective beneficiaries of lower oil.

GS remains overweight the US on valuations versus history and versus other markets when adjusted for growth and volatility, and underweight Europe. Lower oil helps European economies but hurts earnings growth, valuations have not fallen as much as elsewhere, and government debt and the political calendar add risk. Biggest risks are the bond market, oil, AI capex and narrow breadth.

GS Commodities 2027 Outlook recommends a positive commodities allocation. The base case of further energy moderation implies near-zero BCOM total return after 26% YTD, but commodities still hedge a Mideast supply shock or cold winter, and equities and bonds have been unusually sensitive to oil over the past six months. Structural support comes from US-China AI and power competition, with copper forecast at $15,600/t and gold at $4,650/toz by December 2027.

Mericle's 2027 US outlook calls for GDP growth of 2.4%, above consensus, a stable labor market with wage growth around 3.5%, and core PCE inflation falling to 2.4. GS forecasts two more 25bp Fed hikes in December 2026 and March 2027 to a peak of 4.25-4.5%, then gradual cuts to 3.25-3.5% starting at the November 2027 meeting.

GS Prime Brokerage: hedge funds net sold US equities for a second straight week. Macro products (index and ETF) were net bought for a third week, with US-listed ETF shorts down 8.6%, the largest covering in 7 months. Single stocks were heavily net sold (-1.7 SDs), mainly through short sales, with 8 of 11 sectors net sold. Info Tech was the most net sold sector again and its US long/short ratio of 1.5 is the lowest on record since 2016.

Financials was the most net sold US sector in SD terms (-2.2 SDs), the largest percentage selling in 8 months and in the 99th percentile on a 5-year lookback. Nearly all subsectors except Large Cap Banks were net sold, led by Transaction and Payment Processing, Capital Markets, Consumer Finance and Insurance. Consumer Discretionary was the most net bought US sector (+1.0 SDs), while Consumer Staples was heavily net sold (-2.0 SDs), driven by short sales.

Hedge fund performance for the week: fundamental L/S managers up 1.1% (alpha -0.3%) and systematic L/S up 3%. Month to date, fundamental is up 0.6% and systematic up 1.5%. Year to date, fundamental is up 9.7% (alpha +7.1%) and systematic up 17.7%.

Last week's flows: equities closed lower as broader semis and AI thematics caught down to NVDA, with the desk quoting Callahan that the semis rubber band got stretched too far. Macro has gotten tougher again, with VIX at 20, the 10-year back at 5.13% after hot CPI, USD breaking out and oil back in the high $90s. NVDA shed about $500bn of market cap while AMD and AVGO combined added about $500bn or more, and long-only clients supplied NVDA while rotating into hyperscalers and other large-cap tech. Long-only and hedge fund cohorts both finished as moderate net sellers.

China's October retail sales and industrial production both missed, as did Japan's Q3 GDP. Iran targeted a US air defense radar at a base in Bahrain with drones for the second time in three days, ahead of Trump's meetings with Xi and Putin on the sidelines of APEC.

market_movers.rationale: NVDA is down 2.6% pre-market ahead of Tuesday's EPS print, with the market weighing CEO succession, support for Neoclouds and chip export rules. This is the desk's description of a catalyst, not a rating or target change.

sector_views.rationale: Coppersmith would use weakness to add rather than chase rallies, and GS Research argues the selloff has gone too far (basket at 11x 2028 earnings vs about 16x for the S&P). He also expects rotation beyond infrastructure next year, and AI spending growth is peaking.
GS Equities Strategy sees value within Growth sectors of technology, especially hyperscalers, after recent rotations.
GS Equities Strategy favors selective US consumer exposure that should get relief from potentially lower oil prices and bond yields. Hedge funds were also net buyers last week.

GS favors selective defensives that benefit from lower bond yields rather than a broad defensive shift: Europe Utilities and Telecoms, US Healthcare and consistent buyback names, and Asian power companies.
US valuations are attractive versus history and versus other markets when adjusted for growth and volatility.

Lower oil helps the economy but hurts earnings growth, valuations have not fallen as much as elsewhere, and government debt and a heavy political calendar raise risk. GS favors Telecoms, Utilities, UK Real Estate, the DAX and Retailers within Europe.
GS recommends a positive allocation as a hedge against energy and food supply shocks and for structural US-China AI and power demand, though the base case is near-zero BCOM total return in 2027.
No GS view stated. Hedge funds net sold Financials heavily last week (-2.2 SDs, 99th percentile of selling on a 5-year lookback), with Large Cap Banks the exception.

tension_points.bull_case: Positioning is light, with CTAs near max short in NDX and the US Info Tech long/short ratio at a record low, so little positive news could spark a squeeze. The GS AI Semis basket trades at 11x 2028 earnings versus nearly 16x for the S&P despite consensus growth of 31%, and GS Research says much of the selloff has gone too far.
tension_points.bear_case: AI spending growth is peaking and financing is getting more expensive. NVDA leadership uncertainty raises questions on capex cycle duration, support for Neoclouds and export rules, and investors may already be pricing in cuts to earnings estimates.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI capex disappointing because of capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress or weaker demand, which the report lists as a 2027 risk.

tension_points.bull_case: Lower oil prices provide an important boost to European economies, as Europe is the clearest beneficiary of lower energy prices.
tension_points.bear_case: Lower oil also hurts European earnings growth, valuations have not fallen as much as in other regions, and government debt and a heavy political calendar add risk, so GS stays underweight Europe.
